name: pullback within relative trend
idea: Rank names by vol-adjusted relative momentum from 26 to 4 weeks ago plus the inverse of their vol-adjusted relative move over the last 4 weeks, betting that leaders pulling back are near relative bottoms and laggards bouncing are near relative tops.
hypothesis: The baselines point to two effects with opposite signs at different horizons. Intermediate relative momentum (26w skip 4) is positive in all six cells. The most recent month behaves like reversal: skip0 is mostly worse than skip4, especially in AI 4w, and rs_mom is negative everywhere. Mixing them in a single return window, as mom 12w skip0 does, cancels them out and gives inconsistent signs. Separating them tests one economic story. Trends in relative strength persist because information diffuses slowly. Short-term relative moves overshoot, through liquidity and flow-driven exhaustion, and then partly revert within 1-3 months. So the best entries are short-term pullbacks inside established relative uptrends (relative bottoms), and the worst are short-term rallies inside relative downtrends (relative tops). Each component is ranked across names on each date, so neither scale dominates and no full-sample statistics are used. If this fails while plain momentum holds, short-term reversal is not robust at the sector or ETF level. If it fails only in the Sectors cells, reversal there is weaker than the baselines suggest.

name: frog-in-pan continuity + pullback 26s4
idea: Rank-sum of three parts: vol-adjusted 26w-skip-4w relative momentum, the continuity of that momentum (how evenly the up or down weeks were spread through the window, the inverse of information discreteness), and the negative last-4w relative return. It bets on smooth, steady relative trends whose latest month pulled back.
hypothesis: The last candidate (+0.75, same sign in all six cells) showed that relative momentum combined with short-term reversal is the most robust structure so far. Its weakest cells were the Sectors ones. Da, Gurun and Warachka's frog-in-the-pan result is that momentum built from many small, steady moves is underreacted to by inattentive investors and keeps going. Momentum built from a few large jumps is noticed, gets crowded and tends to exhaust. An information-discreteness term should therefore separate trends that persist from trends that are about to top or bottom. I measure it as sign(momentum) × (share of negative weeks − share of positive weeks) over the same 22 weeks as the momentum window. If continuity carries information, the score should rise above the pullback candidate, mainly in the 13-week cells and in the ETF universes. If it does not rise, smoothness of the relative path adds nothing beyond vol-adjusted momentum at sector and industry level.

name: frog-in-pan continuity momentum 26s4
idea: Combines two cross-sectional ranks: 26-week-skip-4 relative momentum, and the net share of up-days versus down-days in daily returns relative to the benchmark over the same window. It bets that trends built from many small consistent gains keep outperforming and that steady bleeders keep lagging.
hypothesis: The 26w-skip4 momentum baselines are the only signals that are positive in all six cells (+0.54), but they are weak in the sector cells. The frog-in-the-pan literature (Da, Gurun & Warachka) argues that investors under-react to information that arrives gradually in many small moves and react fully to salient jumps. So relative trends made of many small consistent days should persist. Jump-driven ones, such as one-off re-ratings or squeezes that make an apparent top or bottom, should mean-revert. Counting the share of relative up-days separates the two kinds of trend at the same total return, which should raise the momentum IC most where single shocks dominate: AI stocks and narrow industry ETFs. If this fails while plain momentum holds, the persistence lies in the size of the move, not in how continuous it is. That would argue against the limited-attention story at the sector level. Daily data is used when the benchmark's daily close can be found; otherwise the code falls back to weekly up/down counts.

name: 52w-high anchor skip4 + continuity + pullback
idea: Rank-sum of vol-scaled distance of the relative-strength ratio (lagged 4w) from its own 52-week high, the frog-in-pan path continuity of the 26s4 trend, and the negative last-4w relative return: names anchored near their relative highs with smooth trends and a recent dip outperform.
hypothesis: George-Hwang anchoring: investors under-react to news that pushes a price near its 52-week high, so nearness to the high predicts continuation better than raw window returns, which depend noisily on the start point (the 26w/52w momentum baselines disagree across sectors and AI). The best candidates so far (+0.75, +0.77) show the pullback (rev4) and continuity components add consistently. This tests whether swapping the raw 26s4 return for an anchor-based trend measure, computed on the relative ratio and scaled by its own volatility so high-vol names are not penalised for being naturally further from highs, strengthens the trend leg, especially in the sector cells where 26w momentum is weakest.

name: daily frog-in-pan continuity + pullback 26s4
idea: Rank-sum of vol-adjusted 26w-skip4 relative momentum, path continuity measured on daily relative-to-benchmark returns over the same skip window (negative information discreteness, about 110 obs instead of 22), and negative last-4w relative return. Smooth relative trends with a recent pullback outperform.
hypothesis: Adding weekly information discreteness to the pullback-in-trend signal raised the sector cells sharply (Sectors4w +0.54 to +1.03), which supports the frog-in-the-pan story. Investors underreact to trends built from many small moves and overreact to a few large jumps. The original Da-Gurun-Warachka measure uses daily returns, while our version used 22 weekly signs, a very noisy estimate of a fraction: its standard error is about 0.1, against a cross-sectional spread of similar size. Counting daily relative-up versus relative-down days over the same 22-week window, skipping the last 4 weeks, should measure gradual information flow more precisely. If the effect is real, precision should lift all cells, especially the weak AI13w cell. If the score falls, either daily noise (bid-ask, FX for foreign names) swamps the signal, or the weekly gain was luck. Both outcomes are informative. It falls back to weekly signs if daily data or the benchmark column is unavailable.

name: volume-conditioned pullback + continuity 26s4
idea: Frog-in-pan composite (vol-adjusted 26w-skip4 relative momentum plus path continuity), with the 4-week reversal leg weighted up when the recent move came on low dollar volume relative to the name's own history and down when it came on heavy volume.
hypothesis: The best candidates so far combine a smooth medium-term relative trend with fading the last 4 weeks. Short-term reversal is usually read as a liquidity-provision premium. Work since Conrad-Hameed-Niden and Gervais-Kaniel-Mingelgrin finds that low-volume moves reverse while high-volume moves carry information and persist. So a quiet pullback inside a relative trend should snap back, and a heavy-volume break should not be faded. Volume is still unused in the log, so this tests one participation hypothesis on top of the strongest base. It uses dollar volume (volume x close) against the name's own trailing 4w/26w history, so splits and local-currency share counts cancel. If the score does not improve on +0.77, or the AI 13w cell stays weak, then volume adds nothing to the reversal leg at weekly ETF and sector frequency.
